facts.fact_text: Immediately after the announcement of the preliminary results of the 19 February 2008 Armenian presidential election, Mr Ter-Petrosyan called on his supporters to gather at Freedom Square (also known as Opera Square) in central Yerevan to protest against alleged irregularities in the election process.
From 20 February 2008 onwards, nationwide daily protest rallies were held by Mr Ter-Petrosyan's supporters, with their main meeting place being Freedom Square and the surrounding park in Yerevan.
The rallies at Freedom Square, held during the daytime and late into the night, attracted at times tens of thousands of people.
Several hundred demonstrators stayed at Freedom Square around the clock, having set up a camp.
The applicant was an active participant in the rallies at Freedom Square and was often on the podium.
On 29 February 2008 the rallies at Freedom Square were still in full swing.
On the night of 29 February 2008 the applicant camped at Freedom Square.

The applicant alleged that the several hundred demonstrators camping at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008 were mostly still asleep when the police arrived, although some were awake, having been informed in advance about the arrival of a large number of police officers.

The applicant alleged that Mr Ter-Petrosyan was also at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008 and addressed the demonstrators, saying: "We see that police forces have arrived at the square. Please, do not have any contact with them and do not touch them in any way. Please keep your distance from them. Let us wait and see what they want from us. If they have something to tell us, we are ready to listen. Please, be patient and peaceful".

During the questioning on 2 March 2008, the applicant submitted that he had not committed any offence and had been participating in a peaceful demonstration at Freedom Square when, at around 6.30 a.m., thousands of police officers had started beating peaceful demonstrators with rubber batons without prior warning or orders to disperse.

During the questioning on 2 March 2008, the applicant admitted his participation in the demonstrations and marches but stated that he had stayed at Freedom Square around the clock only on 29 February 2008.

During the questioning on 2 March 2008, the applicant stated that he had never seen the demonstrators with any weapons or ammunition, that the demonstrations had been peaceful and accompanied with song and dance, and that nobody had given any orders to resist the police.

Section 2 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the concept of a public event includes peaceful assemblies, rallies, marches (parades) and demonstrations (including sit-ins).

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that the 1 March 2008 events started with the forcible termination of the peaceful sit-in at Freedom Square, when at 6.40 a.m. police officers wearing anti-riot gear and carrying shields and batons attacked the demonstrators who were at Freedom Square.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report quoted the OSCE/ODIHR report as stating: "From 21 February to early morning on 1 March protesters held a peaceful, though not formally authorised, assembly (and tent camp) in Freedom Square in Yerevan and conducted numerous peaceful processions. Speakers at the assembly announced that their aim was to annul and repeat the election. Until 1 March, the authorities overall tolerated the protests."

Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe Resolution 1609 (2008) stated that the violations and shortcomings observed in the 19 February 2008 Armenian presidential election raised questions among a part of the Armenian public with regard to the credibility of the outcome of the election, and that this lack of public confidence was the basis for the peaceful protests – held without prior official notification – that ensued after the announcement of the preliminary results, and which were tolerated by the authorities for ten days.

The European Parliament's Resolution of 13 March 2008 stated that opposition supporters began peaceful rallies on 20 February 2008 in Yerevan to protest against the election result and demand a rerun, and that on the evening of 1 March 2008, after eleven days of protest by opposition supporters, violence erupted when police moved into Freedom Square in central Yerevan to disperse the protesters camped out in tents, leaving eight people dead, including one police officer, and dozens injured.

The applicant alleged that suddenly, without any prior warning or orders to disperse, the police forces, shouting loudly, attacked the demonstrators at Freedom Square, most of whom were still asleep in their tents, violently beating them with rubber batons and destroying the camp.
The applicant alleged that within a few minutes no demonstrator remained at Freedom Square, since everybody, including the applicant, had tried to save themselves by fleeing.
The applicant alleged that he and other activists were then pursued by the police through the streets and arrested.

According to a handwritten document entitled "the record of bringing-in", the applicant was "brought in" to Kentron Police Station on 1 March 2008 at around 6.30 a.m. by three police officers, E.R., H.S. and A.A., from 1 Grigor Lusavorich Street.

The record of bringing-in stated that the applicant was brought to Kentron Police Station "for organising unauthorised demonstrations at Freedom Square in support of Mr Ter-Petrosyan, resisting police officers and disobeying their lawful orders".
At around 10.30 p.m. on 1 March 2008 the investigator drew up a record of the applicant's arrest by filling in the relevant template, indicating "10.30 p.m." as the time of the applicant's arrest.

On 3 March 2008 the applicant was formally charged under Articles 225.1 § 2 and 316 § 2, as well as Articles 301 and 318 § 1 of the Armenian Criminal Code, within the scope of criminal case no. 62202608.
The Kentron and Nork-Marash District Court of Yerevan decided to allow the investigator's application and order the applicant's detention for a period of two months.
On 23 October 2008 the Yerevan Criminal Court found the applicant guilty under Article 235 § 4 and Article 316 §§ 1 and 2 of the Armenian Criminal Code.
The Yerevan Criminal Court sentenced the applicant under Article 316 § 2 of the Armenian Criminal Code to five years' imprisonment.

The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that after the announcement of the preliminary results of the 19 February 2008 presidential election, Mr Levon Ter-Petrosyan, members of parliament K.S. and S.M., the chief editor of Haykakan Zhamanak daily newspaper N.P., and others organised and held mass public events at Yerevan's Freedom Square in violation of the procedure prescribed by law and incited disobedience to the decisions ordering an end to the events held in violation of the procedure prescribed by law.

The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that on 1 March 2008 at around 6 a.m., when the police took measures aimed at forcibly ending the public events held in violation of the procedure prescribed by law in compliance with the requirements of section 14 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the organisers and participants of the events, disobeying the lawful orders of the police officers who were performing their official duties, committed a life- and health-threatening assault on them with clubs, metal rods and other adapted objects, causing the police officers injuries of varied severity.

Article 225.1 § 2 of the Armenian Criminal Code (2003) provides that inciting disobedience to an order to terminate a public event held in violation of the procedure prescribed by law is punishable by a fine of between 300 and 500 times the minimum wage or detention of up to three months.

Article 235 § 4 of the Armenian Criminal Code (2003) provides that illegal carrying of a gas, bladed or missile weapon is punishable by a fine of between 200 and 600 times the minimum wage or detention of between one and three months or imprisonment for a period not exceeding two years.

Article 316 § 1 of the Armenian Criminal Code (2003) provides that non-life-threatening or non-health-threatening assault or threat of such assault on a public official or his or her next-of-kin, connected with the performance of his or her official duties, is punishable by a fine of between 300 and 500 times the minimum wage or detention of up to one month or imprisonment for a period not exceeding five years.

Article 316 § 2 of the Armenian Criminal Code (2003) provides that a life-threatening or a health-threatening assault on a public official or his or her next-of-kin, connected with the performance of their duties, is punishable by imprisonment for a period from five to ten years.
Article 225.1 § 1 of the Armenian Criminal Code (2003) prescribes a penalty for organising and holding a public event in violation of the procedure prescribed by law.

Section 10 §§ 1, 2 and 4 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that, except for cases when a non-mass public event spontaneously turns into a mass public event, mass public events may be held only after notifying the competent authority in writing.

Section 10 § 4 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the organisers shall submit a written notification of the intention to hold a mass public event to the head of the local authority where the event is to be held or to the Mayor of Yerevan, if the public event is to be held in Yerevan, not later than five working days and not earlier than twenty days before the planned date of the event.

Section 14 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the police are entitled to decide to terminate a public event and to order the organisers to terminate the event, by allowing them a reasonable time-limit to do so, if, inter alia, the mass public event is being held without notification, except for the cases in which a non-mass public event spontaneously turns into a mass public event.

Section 14 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the police are entitled to terminate forcibly a public event only if (a) the order to terminate an event is not immediately announced to the participants by the organiser; or (b) the order to terminate the public event has not been complied with within the fixed time-limit and its continuation poses a real threat to the life and health of others, State and public security, public order or public or private property.

Section 14 of the Armenian Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act (2004-2011) provides that the police, before forcibly terminating an event, are obliged to inform the participants at least twice over a loudspeaker about the order to terminate the public event and to fix a reasonable time-limit for its termination, and that if the public event is not terminated within such a time-limit, the police are entitled to terminate the event forcibly, using lawful means.

The Government claimed that the reason for the police operation of 1 March 2008 at Freedom Square was information obtained on 29 February 2008 by the Armenian Police and National Security Service, according to which a large number of weapons, including metal rods, wooden clubs, firearms, grenades and explosives, were to be distributed to the protesters to incite provocative actions and mass disorder in Yerevan on 1 March 2008.
The Government claimed that the police operation of 1 March 2008 aimed to verify the intelligence information about weapons being distributed to protesters.

The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that a number of participants in the mass events at Freedom Square illegally possessed and carried illegally obtained arms and ammunition.

The decision instituting criminal case no. 62202508 stated that on 1 March 2008 at around 6 a.m., when the police took measures aimed at forcibly ending the public events held in violation of the procedure prescribed by law in compliance with the requirements of section 14 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the organisers and participants of the events, disobeying the lawful orders of the police officers who were performing their official duties, committed a life- and health-threatening assault on them with clubs, metal rods and other adapted objects, causing the police officers injuries of varied severity.

The Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police's letter of 27 March 2008 stated that the police operation of 1 March 2008 was based on intelligence information received the previous day by the police and the national security service, according to which a large quantity of metal rods, wooden clubs, firearms, grenades and explosives was to be distributed to the demonstrators in order to instigate mass disorder.
The Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police's letter of 27 March 2008 stated that the aim of the 1 March 2008 operation was to verify the intelligence information and to inspect the area.

The supplemented charge stated that the applicant, having regularly participated in the unauthorised demonstrations held following the presidential election, had been present at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008 at around 7 a.m. when some of the demonstrators, using makeshift clubs, rods and other dangerous objects, had assaulted the police officers after the latter had demanded to be allowed to verify the information concerning the possession of arms and ammunition by the demonstrators.

The Yerevan Criminal Court found it established that in the period preceding 1 March 2008 intelligence information was received by the Armenian Police and the National Security Service that the demonstrators gathered at Yerevan's Freedom Square had in their possession firearms, ammunition, clubs, rods and other objects for the purpose of causing physical injuries and violence.

The Yerevan Criminal Court found it established that on 1 March 2008 at around 7 a.m. police officers demanded the persons gathered at Yerevan's Freedom Square to allow them to verify the above information by inspecting the area, and that this demand was announced out loud several times.

Please, do not have any contact with them and do not touch them in any way. Please keep your distance from them. Let us wait and see what they want from us. If they have something to tell us, we are ready to listen. Please, be patient and peaceful".
The applicant alleged that after Mr Ter-Petrosyan's address there was silence for about a minute, by which time the police forces had already encircled Freedom Square with a triple cordon.

The applicant alleged that suddenly, without any prior warning or orders to disperse, the police forces, shouting loudly, attacked the demonstrators at Freedom Square, most of whom were still asleep in their tents, violently beating them with rubber batons and destroying the camp.

The Government claimed that the police operation of 1 March 2008 aimed to verify the intelligence information about weapons being distributed to protesters.

The Government claimed that members of the relevant police force, without being equipped with any protective gear, arrived at Freedom Square where about 800 to 900 demonstrators armed with metal rods and wooden clubs had gathered waiting for the police.

The Government claimed that the demonstrators attacked the police officers on 1 March 2008, hitting them and throwing stones, pointed metal objects and Molotov cocktails at them, as a result of which numerous police officers were injured.

According to the records of inspection of the scene, a number of different objects were found at Freedom Square and the surrounding park on 1 March 2008, including pistols, cartridges, grenades and other explosives, wooden and rubber clubs, metal rods and other metal objects having a spiky, hedgehog-like shape.

The Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police's letter of 27 March 2008 stated that the aim of the 1 March 2008 operation was to verify the intelligence information and to inspect the area.

The Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police's letter of 27 March 2008 stated that a number of unarmed police officers had entered Opera Square (Freedom Square) where they were attacked by 800-900 demonstrators armed with metal rods and wooden clubs, who were expecting the arrival of the police.
The Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police's letter of 27 March 2008 stated that the police officers were beaten and stones, pointed metal objects and Molotov cocktails were thrown at them.

The Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police's letter of 27 March 2008 stated that in order to prevent the disorder, an on-the-spot decision had been taken to engage the auxiliary police forces, which had been deployed earlier on the approaches to Freedom Square and had been equipped with helmets, shields and rubber batons.

The Deputy Chief of the Armenian Police's letter of 27 March 2008 stated that the operation was carried out between 7 and 7.30 a.m. and was followed by a search, as a result of which numerous specially adapted metal objects, arms, ammunition and Molotov cocktails were found.

During the questioning on 2 March 2008, the applicant submitted that he had not committed any offence and had been participating in a peaceful demonstration at Freedom Square when, at around 6.30 a.m., thousands of police officers had started beating peaceful demonstrators with rubber batons without prior warning or orders to disperse.

During the questioning on 2 March 2008, the applicant stated that he had never seen the demonstrators with any weapons or ammunition, that the demonstrations had been peaceful and accompanied with song and dance, and that nobody had given any orders to resist the police.

During the questioning on 2 March 2008, the applicant stated that orders to resist the police would have been pointless anyway, since the police had entered the square covertly and started assaulting the demonstrators with rubber batons.

Police officer A.Arsh. submitted before the Yerevan Criminal Court that on 1 March 2008, when the police asked the demonstrators gathered at Freedom Square to allow them to carry out an inspection for weapons, the demonstrators had reacted violently, and that the applicant had attacked him and hit him twice on the head with a stick, after which he had fled.

Police officer A.Aru. submitted before the Yerevan Criminal Court that he had seen the applicant attack police officer A.Arsh. and hit him on the head with a stick, and that he had thereafter continued to perform his duty in the area of Arshakunyats Street, where he had noticed the applicant, asked him to go with him to a police station, but the applicant had hit him several times on the chest, kicked his shield and fled.
The applicant denied his guilt before the Yerevan Criminal Court and submitted that even if he had participated in the demonstrations held from 20 February 2008, he had done nothing illegal.

The applicant submitted before the Yerevan Criminal Court that he and his co-thinkers at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008 had found out about the forthcoming arrival of the police several hours in advance, and that after the police had arrived, he had not hit anyone and had tried to escape.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that the 1 March 2008 events started with the forcible termination of the peaceful sit-in at Freedom Square, when at 6.40 a.m. police officers wearing anti-riot gear and carrying shields and batons attacked the demonstrators who were at Freedom Square.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that the 1 March 2008 intervention was justified with the argument that on 29 February the police and the National Security Service had received intelligence information according to which arms were building up at Freedom Square, and that in order to render the situation harmless, in the morning of 1 March the police undertook an operation intended to seize those socially-dangerous materials.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that the campaign headquarters of Mr Ter-Petrosyan and the opposition Heritage Party both insisted that the objective of the measures of the morning of 1 March 2008 was, under the disguise of an inspection of the area, to terminate by force the peaceful demonstrations that had been ongoing for ten days, to remove the persons participating in the sit-in and to ban further demonstrations at Freedom Square.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report noted contradictions in the statements released by the Prosecutor General's Office, including that the request lodged by the Prosecutor General on 4 March 2008 stated "the objective of the police was to carry out an operation aimed at seizing arms, which deteriorated into a clash", while the press release issued by the Prosecutor General's Office on 1 March stated "the objective of the police was to terminate forcibly the assembly at around 6 a.m. on 1 March".

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report raised the question of how it happened that at around 6.30 a.m. on 1 March 2008, in a matter of just minutes, the police was able to mobilise numerous units wearing anti-riot gear and carrying shields and batons, if the only objective was to perform an inspection of the area.

The Armenian Ombudsman's Report stated that while it is true that every day prior to 1 March the police announced over loudspeakers that the demonstration was unlawful and ordered the demonstrators to end it, no such order was made in the morning of 1 March 2008 and no time-limit was given to the demonstrators to end the demonstration as required by section 14 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that after nine days of peaceful demonstrations on Opera Square (Freedom Square), the national police and security forces tried to disperse the protesters on 1 March 2008, and that clashes occurred between the police and security forces and the demonstrators in front of Myasnikyan's monument and the French Embassy, which resulted in the death of eight persons.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that the Head of Police explained that the police had received information that the demonstrators were arming themselves with weapons and ammunition, and that the initial intent was also to move them to another location in the city to avoid problems of public transport and sanitation.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that the search operation reportedly started early Saturday morning at approximately 6.30 a.m., during which tents were taken down and people were beaten and injured, and that demonstrators started resisting and clashes broke out.

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights' report of 20 March 2008 stated that it seemed clear that excessive use of force was used by police and the security forces, as confirmed by the sheer number of injured persons and passing civilians registered in the hospitals as well as found in places of detention, having beating marks, concussion and open scars on their skulls.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that statements taken from demonstrators and bystanders suggested that the first police action in the early morning of 1 March 2008 against the Freedom Square tent encampment entailed excessive use of force, without warning and in the absence, at the start, of resistance.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that according to the first deputy police chief A.M., the police had arrived at Freedom Square on 1 March 2008 to conduct a search, acting on information that demonstrators had been arming themselves with metal rods, and possibly firearms, in preparation for committing acts of violent protest, and that initially a group of 25-30 police officers, including experts and investigators, were sent to do the search.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that according to the first deputy police chief A.M., when the group tried to conduct the search, the protesters turned aggressive and resisted police with wooden sticks and iron bars, resulting in injuries to several policemen, and that more police had to be deployed and had to use force to disperse the crowd, with the operation lasting about 30 minutes and 10 policemen sustaining injuries.

Human Rights Watch's report stated that according to multiple witnesses, even before Mr Ter-Petrosyan finished his address, police advanced towards the demonstrators in several lines, beating their truncheons against their plastic shields, making no audible demand for anyone to disperse nor giving any indication of the purpose of their presence, and then without any warning, riot police attacked the demonstrators, using rubber truncheons, iron sticks, and electric shock batons.
